newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Arab foreign ministers skeptical about summit.
newsitem.headline: Arab foreign ministers skeptical about summit.

text.p: Arab foreign ministers expressed scepticism on Monday about the outcome of a planned meeting in Washington between Palestinian President Yasser Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
But they appeared more upbeat about the benefits of Arafat's conferring with President Bill Clinton, host of the summit, which is to begin on Tuesday.
The Washington talks are an attempt to put the Middle East peace process back on track after last week's clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops in which about 70 people were killed.

After a meeting of Arab foreign ministers attending the current General Assembly session, Arab League Secretary-General Esmat Abdel-Meguid told reporters they had agreed to set up a "mechanism" to monitor developments in the peace process.

The group will consist of the foreign ministers of Egypt, chairman of the last Arab summit, Algeria, chairman of the Arab council of foreign ministers, Syria and Lebanon; representatives of the Palestinians and the Gulf Cooperation Council; and Abdel-Meguid.

Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, who chaired Monday's meeting, said it had been agreed that the Middle East peace process should proceed on the basis of the principle of "land for peace" and relevant Security Council resolutions.

He cited resolutions 242 and 338, adopted after the 1967 and 1973 Arab-Israeli wars and embodying the idea of "land for peace," and resolution 425 of 1978, calling for Israel's complete withdrawal from Lebanon, where it still retains a so-called security zone to prevent attacks against northern Israel.

Referring to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's decision not to attend the Washington meeting, to which Jordan's King Hussein has accepted an invitation, Lebanese Foreign Minister Faris Bouez told reporters:

"We understand very positively the absence of President Mubarak from this meeting. We consider that the presence of Arafat for such a meeting with President Clinton to expose the problems and to give details about what is happening is also very positive.

"But we don't think any meeting between Arafat and Netanyahu will really be very positive unless it will be prepared before and unless Mr. Arafat will be sure to have some guarantees concerning the (resumption) of political talks concerning Palestine."
Bouez said Netanyahu often reaped benefits from such meetings and tried to send messages to international public opinion that "blank out" what is happening in Palestine.
"It is why we are very cautious about such meetings which are not sufficiently prepared before," Bouez said.
"And we are (making a distinction) between accepting the invitation to Washington to meet with President Clinton and/or to accept a meeting with Netanyahu unless some guarantees are addressed."
The Arab League's U.N. observer, Mahmoud Aboul-Nasr, said there was "an appreciation for the invitation (to Washington) and the effort." "We wish them well," he said.
"However, Israel in advance objected to most of what was in the Security Council resolution adopted just two days ago," he added.

He was referring to a resolution adopted late on Saturday, with only the United States abstaining. It implicitly called for the closing of a controversial archaeological tunnel in Jerusalem, the immediate resumption of the Middle East peace process "on its agreed basis," the timely implementation of agreements already reached, and the ensuring of the safety and protection of Palestinian civilians.

Saying Israel had "put President Clinton in a very difficult position," Aboul-Nasr added: "We hope that (the meeting) will succeed and hope that President Clinton will be able to convince Israel not to continue (on its present path) and to abide by the ... unanimous will of the international community, which was very clear during the Security Council debate."
